**Network Scanning**

**Objective:**

This lab is to help get you used to using the programs NMap/ZenMap and netcat for network scanning. Network scanning can reveal a lot about the weak spots for a network, allowing us to patch them before they can be exploited.

**Setup:**

1. Before beginning your Nmap scans, **start a WireShark capture and filter for your IP address**.

![][image1]

**Nmap \- Instructions:**

1. Start ZenMap, then target 10.0.17.1-254 with a ping scan (beneath the Profile tab).
![][image2]
2. Click “scan”. You should get a list of devices that are responding to the ping.
3. Stop your wireshark capture and save it.
4. Next, choose a target range that includes 3 of the hosts that were up and scan. Make sure to choose a range that includes the one with the most open ports.
   ![][image3]

5. Select Quick scan plus under profile. Be sure to note the commands being used for NMap in the command window.

   1. Copy the command in the below, then break down what the options are. To find the options, select the Profile tab at the top of the screen, then Edit. Look through all the tabs to see all the options.

   ![][image4]

   2. **Deliverable 1:** Below, create a table with the options and descriptions of what they do.
![Pasted image 20261019122420.png](/img/user/SEC-250/Assignments/Nmap%20lab/_assets/Pasted%20image%2020261019122420.png)

| Option                | What it does                                       |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| nmap                  | Runs nmap                                          |
| -sV             | Probe open ports to determine service/version info |
| -T4             | Sets timing template to 4                          |
| -O              | Enable OS detection                                |
| -F              | Fast mode - Scan fewer ports than the default scan |
| --version-light | Limit to most likely probes (intensity 2)          |
| 10.0.17.9-11          | Tells nmap to scan 10.0.17.9 to .11                |

2. Start a new Wireshark capture
3. Launch the scan.

5. Stop your wireshark capture and save it.

6. Find a partner. Both of you should start a new service on the VM using Netcat.

   7. Open up an instance of Terminal with Root permissions.

   8. Then, run the command **netcat \-l \-p 5555**. This will start an instance of netcat in listening mode. If you wish, you can choose a port between 1025 and 65535\.

![][image5]

3. **Leave this window open**. If it’s closed, the program will stop running. Then, run an Intense Scan with UDP in Zenmap of your IP.

10. Start a new Wireshark capture.

11. Scan each other with an Intense Scan with UDP profile. *Note: **Only let the service scan run for about 15 mins. Then cancel. A full UDP scan in our environment took an hour while no one else was running a scan… so don’t do that.***

**Deliverable 5: Research & Reflection**

1. From what you saw, what do you believe are the top 3 security risks on the scanned systems? How would you begin to address these vulnerabilities?
**I believe the top three security issues are the number of open ports, the services behind those ports, and the OS version of the devices. First of all I would close all ports that are not being used on each host. Then i would disable and remove any un-used services. Finally I would update each host to the latest software verisons.**

2. How does network scanning help both attackers and defenders? What does this tell you about regular security audits?
**Network scanning helps attackers find out what is online and open on a network in order to find something to exploit. It also helps defenders find open ports in order to close them up and increase security. This tells me that regular security audits can use the same tools as attackers in order to make the network more secure.**
3. What are the key differences between “Quick scan plus” and “Intense scan plus UDP”, and when would you use each in a real world scenario?
**The key difference is the number of ports scanned. Quick scan only scans commonly open ports while intense scan scans all ports. Quick scan would be used in the real world for scanning a large network. Intense scan might be used for scanning a single device on a network.**
4. Why do you think some ports show as “filtered” instead of “open” or “closed”? What does this tell you about network configuration?
**Filtered shows that something between the scanner and the target interfered with the connection so the scanner couldn't tell weather the port was open or closed. It tells me that there could be a firewall or something in the way blocking traffic on that port.**
5. Why is it important to only scan networks and systems you have permission to scan? What could be the consequences of doing so unauthorized?
**It is important because it would be unethical to scan a network you don't have permission to scan, you could also get in legal trouble for it. It could also cause access issues from a large volume of traffic going over the network.**
